content: Women who are triage-negative based on cytology or visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) should undergo a follow-up HPV test at 12 months. If the HPV test at this follow-up is negative, they can return to the routine screening interval. Summary tables provide detailed guidance on interpreting outcomes, which represent the total events over the lifetime of a cohort of 100,000 women. These outcomes include cervical cancer cases, cervical cancer deaths, pre-cancer treatments, additional pre-term deliveries due to pre-cancer treatments, and the number needed to treat (NNT) to avert a cervical cancer death. The tables also include discounted lifetime costs associated with these interventions. For women living with HIV (WLHIV), screening strategies and intervals are tailored. For example, triage-negative women returning for HPV testing at 24 months instead of 12 months may experience a loss in effectiveness. Variations in screening algorithms, such as primary HPV testing, HPV with 16/18 genotyping, or HPV with VIA or colposcopy triage, are compared in terms of cervical cancer cases, deaths, pre-cancer treatments, and NNT. Post-treatment follow-up for women with a history of CIN3+ involves HPV testing at 12, 24, and 36 months. Women return to routine screening after three consecutive negative tests. Any positive test during follow-up warrants referral for treatment. Screening compliance rates and sensitivity analyses are considered for different follow-up options. For instance, compliance rates for follow-up HPV testing at 12 months are modeled at 90% and 75%, while follow-up at 24 months assumes compliance rates of 70% and 50%. Co-testing with HPV and cytology at 12 months is also an option, with compliance rates modeled similarly. For all positive women, treatment decisions are guided by VIA eligibility or triage results. Women who test positive for HPV types 16/18 are treated based on VIA triage results. Multiple treatments may be required for women needing follow-up. The effectiveness of screening strategies is evaluated based on cervical cancer incidence and mortality reduction, as well as the number of pre-cancer treatments required. Discount rates for effect (0%) and cost (3%) are applied in economic analyses.
